items.prompt: What is a performance improvement plan?
choices: A private note the manager keeps about how a report is doing over time
A scheduled review where teammates rank one another's work each quarter
A written, time-bound statement of acceptable performance
items.explanation: A PIP turns a vague worry into specific written expectations with a deadline.

items.prompt: Why write expectations down instead of repeating them in 1:1s?
choices: So whether they were met becomes a checkable fact
So the report has fewer chances to ask follow-up questions
So the manager avoids bringing it up again
items.explanation: Writing it down makes the answer a fact, not two people's impressions.

items.prompt: Which element does a PIP always include?
choices: A guarantee that the report keeps the role
A defined period with dated checkpoints
A ranking against the rest of the team
items.explanation: The time-bound period and checkpoints are what separate it from ongoing worry.

items.prompt: A PIP is mainly used when what has not worked?
choices: A change of office or team seating
A company-wide hiring freeze
Informal coaching and feedback
items.explanation: It is the step after informal coaching has not closed a real gap.

items.prompt: What does a PIP replace?
choices: The need for the manager to give any support
A vague feeling of falling short
The report's own view of how things are going
items.explanation: It swaps a feeling for a clear yes/no standard.

items.prompt: Which line belongs in a PIP?
choices: Ship the June 15 release on or before its stated date
Show a better attitude toward deadlines in general
Try to be more reliable than you have been
items.explanation: Only the first is specific and checkable.

items.prompt: Who should be able to check whether a PIP goal was met?
choices: Only the manager, using their own judgment
Only HR, working from a later summary
Both people, working from the same facts
items.explanation: A shared, checkable fact is what makes the plan fair.

items.prompt: What should a PIP offer besides expectations?
choices: A promise that the plan will be dropped quietly
Concrete support that the manager commits to giving
A list of other people's mistakes for comparison
items.explanation: A plan with demands and no support reads as a paper trail.

items.prompt: A manager says 'you have two weeks to start performing better' and leaves it there. What is the main thing missing from this as a plan?
choices: A longer window so the report feels less rushed overall
A warning about consequences, stated in more severe terms
A comparison with how teammates have been performing
A written standard that both people can check
items.explanation: The deadline exists, but 'performing better' has no definition. The plan's job is to make the outcome a fact, not a feeling.
items.reference:
Plan vs. impression
vague: 'be more consistent' (an impression)
plan: 'ship Jun 15 on or before its date' (a fact)
plan adds: a period, checkpoints, support
Why: a PIP exists to turn a feeling about performance into a fact both people can check.
items.learnMore:
What a PIP is for

A PIP is not a punishment form. Its job is to define acceptable in checkable terms, give a period and checkpoints, and name the support the manager provides.

Common mistake

Writing demands with no support and no checkpoints, so the plan only reads as a paper trail.
items.reflection: Think of a goal you were once given that was vague. How would you have rewritten it so you could tell, on a specific day, whether you had met it?

items.prompt: A report's work needs rework on most deliveries and nothing has been said formally yet. What is the right first move?
choices: A written 30-day PIP so expectations exist on paper from the start
Direct, specific feedback in the moment, before any formal plan
A team-wide note restating the quality bar for every engineer
A wait of another quarter to collect more data before speaking
items.explanation: A PIP follows informal coaching that has not worked. Even a clear pattern starts with direct feedback; the formal plan is a later step.

items.prompt: Two PIPs cover the same weak delivery record. One says 'be more reliable.' The other says 'flag any at-risk date 3 business days ahead, in writing.' What does the second give that the first cannot?
choices: A yes/no answer that both people can check
A tougher standard that a report is less likely to meet
A way for the manager to avoid writing checkpoint notes
More freedom for the report to choose how to improve
items.explanation: Specificity is not about toughness. It makes 'was it met' a factual question, so the checkpoint cannot become a second argument.

items.prompt: What does the no-surprises principle say?
choices: It must never be the first time the report hears it is serious
The manager should avoid raising any problem until a PIP is ready
The report should be told about every PIP weeks before each review
items.explanation: It says the plan formalizes something already communicated.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, why was the report surprised?
choices: The manager had refused to answer any of their questions
The one mention was gentle and never framed as a warning
The manager had told them the work was excellent
items.explanation: A vague mention reads as coaching, not as a job at risk.

items.prompt: What does the principle test?
choices: How many times the manager spoke about it
Whether the manager felt they had been clear
What the report actually understood from it
items.explanation: It is about the report's understanding, not the manager's intent.

items.prompt: What does a PIP that breaks this principle look like to the report?
choices: Sudden and unfair, even when the problem is quite real
Helpful and well timed, since the report was prepared
Too lenient, given everything that had happened
items.explanation: Sudden reads as unfair whatever the underlying facts are.

items.prompt: Which statement counts as an explicit warning?
choices: Let us try to be a bit more consistent over the next month or so
Deadlines have been a little tight for everyone on the team lately
This is serious and puts your role at risk if it continues
items.explanation: Only the first states the stakes in plain terms.

items.prompt: What is the safest way to confirm the report understood the stakes?
choices: Ask them to say back what they heard
Assume silence means they understood
Send a longer email with more detail
items.explanation: Hearing it said back is how you check understanding, not delivery.

items.prompt: When should the explicit warning happen?
choices: On the same page as the plan's first line
Before any formal PIP exists on paper
After the PIP is already signed
items.explanation: The plan formalizes the warning; it should not be the warning.

items.prompt: What does the principle protect, besides the report?
choices: The manager's right to decide without giving notice
The company's ability to keep records private
The credibility of the process and the manager
items.explanation: A fair process is easier to defend and easier to trust.

items.prompt: A manager says in a 1:1: 'Deadlines have slipped a bit, let us tighten that up.' Six weeks later the same manager opens a PIP. The report says they had no idea it was serious. Who is right?
choices: The manager, because the topic was raised once already
Neither, since tone can never be judged afterwards
The report, because nothing said the role was at risk
The manager, since the report could have asked directly
items.explanation: The principle is about what the report understood. A soft mention that never named the stakes does not meet it, even though words were said.
items.reference:
Said vs. understood
said: 'let us try to be more consistent'
meant: this is a serious problem
understood: normal coaching, nothing at risk
Why: the principle is judged on the report's understanding, so the warning must name the stakes.
items.learnMore:
The no-surprises principle

By the time a PIP starts, the report should already know the performance is a serious problem. The plan formalizes that conversation and time-bounds it; it does not replace it.

Common mistake

Counting a gentle hint as a warning because the topic was technically raised once.
items.reflection: Recall a time you were told something important but did not realize how serious it was until later. What would have made it unmistakable at the time?

items.prompt: A manager has a dated record of six missed deadlines but never told the report the role was at risk. What does the record fix?
choices: It replaces the need for any conversation about the stakes
It shows the report was told simply because it is dated
Nothing; it records events but never delivers the warning
It proves the principle was met as soon as the PIP starts
items.explanation: A trail documents events. It does not by itself deliver the explicit warning that the principle requires.

items.prompt: Which opening line for a PIP meeting best honors the no-surprises principle?
choices: On May 22 I told you this puts your role at risk; here is the plan
I have been thinking about this for a while and today I have decided to act
HR asked me to give you this document and walk you through it
This is a fresh start for you, so please read the plan with an open mind
items.explanation: The line points back to a specific earlier warning. The others present the plan as new, which is exactly the surprise to avoid.

items.prompt: What comes first in a fair sequence?
choices: A formal written plan to the report
An informal, specific signal in the moment
A final decision about the role
items.explanation: The sequence starts with direct feedback, not paperwork.

items.prompt: Which step turns routine coaching into a serious matter?
choices: The explicit warning
The first dated record
The mid-point checkpoint
items.explanation: The warning is where the stakes are named.

items.prompt: If the pattern stops after the informal signal, what happens?
choices: A PIP starts anyway, just for the record
The manager waits another quarter to see
It resolves informally; no PIP
items.explanation: A PIP is a later step, not an automatic one.

items.prompt: Where did the Scenario's manager skip a step?
choices: The informal signal
The explicit warning
The final checkpoint
items.explanation: The mention was never framed as serious.

items.prompt: What follows the explicit warning?
choices: A dated documentation trail
A final decision at once
A team announcement of the issue
items.explanation: The trail starts after the warning and continues forward.

items.prompt: What happens after the formal PIP starts?
choices: A new round of informal signals only
Defined, dated checkpoints in the period
No more reviews until the end date
items.explanation: Checkpoints are built into the plan.

items.prompt: What can happen at the final checkpoint if the bar is met?
choices: A second PIP begins at once
The record is destroyed for privacy
The PIP closes successfully
items.explanation: Meeting the bar ends the plan in writing.

items.prompt: Why does the order of steps matter?
choices: Each step depends on the one before having been understood
It makes the process look more official
It lets the manager avoid hard talks
items.explanation: Skipping a step undermines everything after it.

items.prompt: A manager gave a vague heads-up in March, the pattern continued, and in June the manager wants to start a PIP. Per the sequence, what is the next step?
choices: Start the dated trail and treat March as the warning
Open the PIP now and explain the stakes in its first page
Wait one more month to see whether anything changes by itself
Hold a dedicated conversation naming the stakes plainly
items.explanation: The explicit warning has not happened yet. Documentation and the plan both depend on it.
items.reference:
The fair sequence
A informal signal
D explicit warning (stakes named)
E dated documentation trail
G formal PIP with checkpoints
Why: each later step relies on the earlier one having been understood, so none can be skipped safely.
items.learnMore:
Why the order matters

The warning makes the trail meaningful, and the trail makes the plan defensible. Taking a step out leaves the next one resting on nothing.

Common mistake

Starting the paperwork first and delivering the warning inside the PIP document.
items.reflection: Think of a process you were part of where a step was skipped and the later steps felt unfair. Which step would you have inserted, and where?

items.prompt: Which action is out of order in a fair sequence?
choices: Keeping dated notes after a warning has been given
Writing a formal PIP before the report has been warned
Dropping the process when the pattern stops on its own
Holding a written checkpoint halfway through the period
items.explanation: The plan formalizes something already understood. Putting it before the warning flips the order.

choices: Start over with a new informal signal as if nothing happened
The trail from the warning supports moving to a formal PIP
Skip the PIP and decide using the manager's overall impression
Treat the three good weeks as having ended the matter for good
items.explanation: The second pattern check in the flow sends a continuing pattern to the formal plan, backed by the trail already built.

items.prompt: What is a documentation trail?
choices: A diary of the manager's feelings about the report
A list of every mistake anyone on the team has made
A dated record of examples and conversations
items.explanation: It records facts with dates, not impressions.

items.prompt: When should the trail start?
choices: At the explicit warning, well ahead of the PIP itself
On the day the PIP begins, once it is decided
After the final checkpoint, once results are in
items.explanation: It should predate the plan by weeks.

items.prompt: Which entry is best?
choices: Seems to be slipping a little lately
Missed the Mar 3 deadline by 4 days
Just not at the level we expect
items.explanation: It is dated and specific.

items.prompt: What should the trail include about the report?
choices: Only the points that support the plan
Nothing beyond the misses
Context or explanations they raised
items.explanation: Their side belongs in the record too.

items.prompt: Why does a late-starting trail look bad?
choices: It is harder to type up in a hurry
It makes the PIP seem sudden or retaliatory
It leaves out the date of the warning
items.explanation: Two weeks of notes cannot show an established pattern.

items.prompt: What does the trail show about the warning?
choices: That the warning conversation took place
That the report agreed with every point raised
That the report was upset when it was held
items.explanation: It documents the no-surprises step.

items.prompt: Who benefits from a good trail?
choices: Only the manager, to keep control
Only the company's lawyers, if needed
Both the report and the manager alike
items.explanation: A factual record helps everyone find where things stand.

items.prompt: What should a record avoid?
choices: Dated notes of conversations held
Opinions about the person's character
Specific examples of missed deadlines
items.explanation: Keep it to observable events.

items.prompt: A manager decides on Monday to open a PIP and spends the week writing up the last quarter's problems. What is the main weakness of this record?
choices: It includes too many dates to be easy to read
It leaves out the opinions the manager holds about the report
It covers a whole quarter, which is too long for any record
It was written to justify the plan, not before it
items.explanation: A record created at the point of decision lacks the history that makes the plan look like the next step.
items.reference:
Strong vs. weak entries
strong: 'Mar 7: missed by 4 days; cited unclear specs'
weak: 'seems to be slipping lately'
include: the manager's own corrective steps
Why: dated, specific, two-sided entries turn impressions into a record that can be checked.
items.learnMore:
What a good trail holds

Dated events, specific examples, the explicit-warning conversation, and anything the report raised. It starts at the warning, not at the plan.

Common mistake

Gathering evidence only after deciding to open a PIP, which looks like building a case.
items.reflection: Where in your own work do you keep notes that would be fair to you if someone reviewed them later? What would you add?

items.prompt: Which pair of entries gives the strongest trail for a missed release?
choices: 'Mar 7: missed by 4 days; cited unclear specs' and 'Apr 2: specs clarified in writing'

'March: slow overall' and 'April: slow again, and the dashboard was wrong when delivered to QA'
'Mar 7: late due to poor planning' and 'Apr 2: planning has still not improved at all'
items.explanation: The first pair has dates, a measure, the report's explanation, and the manager's corrective step.

Record it only after the PIP has begun to be fair

items.prompt: Which goal is specific and observable?
choices: A written update every Friday for six weeks
Communicate more openly with the whole team
Be a stronger team player
items.explanation: Only the first can be checked as yes or no.

items.prompt: Why avoid goals like 'improve overall performance'?
choices: They are too easy for most people to meet
Nobody can say if it happened
They take far too long to write down
items.explanation: A vague goal moves the argument to the checkpoint.

items.prompt: What makes a goal checkable?
choices: A strong opinion from the manager
A consensus on how things feel
A fact, a count, or a date on a calendar
items.explanation: Facts can be verified by either side.

items.prompt: Which wording fixes 'be more thorough in reviews'?
choices: Leave a substantive comment on 90% of assigned PRs
Be as thorough as the strongest reviewers on the team
Try your very best on every review that you are given
items.explanation: It gives a measure and a way to check it weekly.

items.prompt: What happens at the checkpoint with a vague goal?
choices: The report passes automatically
The goal is rewritten by HR
The manager and report disagree again
items.explanation: The Scenario's original disagreement repeats.

items.prompt: Who is hurt by a vague goal?
choices: Both sides, the report and also the manager
Only the report, since they carry the risk
Nobody, since it is only a matter of wording
items.explanation: The manager has no defensible answer either.

items.prompt: A goal says 'ship by June 15'. What makes it specific?
choices: It sounds firm and leaves no room
It names a date that can be checked
It is written in a firm, confident tone
items.explanation: A date is a fact.

items.prompt: Should every goal in the PIP have been raised earlier?
choices: No, new goals keep the plan fresh
Only the first one needs to be
Yes, none should be new to the report
items.explanation: A goal that appears for the first time breaks no-surprises.

items.prompt: A PIP says: 'Show more ownership of your projects.' The report asks how they will know whether they met it. What is the most useful rewrite?
choices: Take clear responsibility for the outcome of every project
Demonstrate ownership in a way that the team can see
Ownership will be assessed by the manager at each review
Give a written status update on each project weekly
items.explanation: The rewrite replaces a trait with observable events. The others restate the trait or leave judgment to the manager.
items.reference:
Vague vs. checkable
vague: 'communicate better'
checkable: 'written update every Friday, 6 weeks'
test: can both people answer yes/no from facts?
Why: a goal is fair when meeting it is a question of fact rather than opinion.
items.learnMore:
Making a goal observable

Replace the trait with an event, a count, or a date, and say how it will be checked. Then the final checkpoint is a lookup, not a debate.

Common mistake

Writing demanding goals that sound precise but still depend on the manager's judgment, like 'high quality work'.
items.reflection: Pick a goal you set for yourself that was vague. How could you restate it so a stranger could confirm on a given date whether you reached it?

items.prompt: Which set of three expectations passes the specificity test best?

Be dependable; keep work tidy and well organized; raise issues early enough to help
Hit deadlines; minimize rework where you can; keep stakeholders informed along the way
items.explanation: Each item in the first set has a yes/no answer. The others use qualities that need judgment.

items.prompt: In L3, why was the Apr 2 entry included?
choices: It was the first missed deadline in the year
It shows the manager's corrective step
It was the date the PIP took effect
items.explanation: It answers the report's earlier explanation.

items.prompt: What does a one-sided record look like?
choices: Only the report's failures, no manager actions
Entries from both sides, with dates attached to each
A list with dates, examples, and the sizes of each miss
items.explanation: It reads as building a case.

items.prompt: Why record the report's Mar 7 explanation?
choices: It helps the manager excuse the miss later
It makes the whole list longer and more complete
It shows the process listened to their side
items.explanation: The record should reflect both views.

items.prompt: What did the Apr 2 clarification remove?
choices: The need for any PIP once a pattern is established
The earlier explanation of unclear requirements
The May miss from the record, once resolved
items.explanation: Later misses can no longer be blamed on it.

items.prompt: Before the PIP, what conversation happened?
choices: The explicit warning on May 22
The final review on June 30
The mid-point checkpoint on June 15
items.explanation: It repaired the missing step.

items.prompt: Can the manager backfill entries?
choices: Yes, anything that seems likely enough to include
Yes, only what can honestly be reconstructed
No, the trail may only start from today
items.explanation: Honest reconstruction is fine; invention is not.

items.prompt: What makes the record fair?
choices: It uses stronger language
It is shown only to HR
It includes steps the manager took to help
items.explanation: Fairness shows in the process, not the tone.

items.prompt: Who should the record be fair to?
choices: Both the report and the manager, equally
Only the manager who keeps the trail
Only whoever reads it last of all
items.explanation: A balanced record serves everyone.

items.prompt: A manager's record lists five misses, with dates and sizes, but nothing about requirements being clarified in between. A reviewer asks if the process was fair. What is the likeliest reading?
choices: That the manager was too detailed in recording the misses
That the report would have missed the dates regardless
That the manager built a case rather than tried to help
That the missing step has no bearing on later misses
items.explanation: Leaving out the corrective step makes the record look like a list of grievances.
items.reference:
One-sided vs. two-sided
one-sided: misses only
two-sided: misses + Apr 2 clarification + report's explanation
effect: answers 'was the process fair?'
Why: recording the manager's own steps shows the process tried to help.
items.learnMore:
Why record your own steps

The record has to show that a reasonable explanation was heard and addressed. Then a later miss can be judged on its own.

Common mistake

Treating the explanation as noise and leaving it out of the trail.
items.reflection: Think of a time you reviewed a record of events. What made it feel like fair evidence versus a one-sided story?

items.prompt: The report disputes the Mar 7 entry, saying the miss was caused by changing requirements. The record shows requirements were clarified on Apr 2. What does that clarification actually prove?
choices: That the Mar 7 miss was entirely the report's fault from the beginning
That requirements were never unclear at any point in the project
That the excuse was addressed afterwards, not that Mar 7 was their fault
That the report should not have raised any explanation at all
items.explanation: The clarification removes the excuse going forward. It does not rewrite what caused the first miss.

items.learnMore:
Why record your own steps

The record has to show that a reasonable explanation was heard and addressed. Then a later miss can be judged on its own.

Common mistake

Treating the explanation as noise and leaving it out of the trail.
items.reflection: Think of a time you reviewed a record of events. What made it feel like fair evidence versus a one-sided story?

items.prompt: Which backfilled entry is acceptable?
choices: 'Jan 14: report agreed the March date', per saved meeting notes
'Jan 14: report felt unprepared', recalled from the manager's own memory
'Feb 20: report was disengaged', inferred from how they behaved in meetings
'Mar 1: report ignored warnings', added later to strengthen the record
items.explanation: Backfill only what a source can support. The others add interpretation or events that never happened.
items.reference:
One-sided vs. two-sided
one-sided: misses only
two-sided: misses + Apr 2 clarification + report's explanation
effect: answers 'was the process fair?'
Why: recording the manager's own steps shows the process tried to help.

items.prompt: What does a checkpoint note record?
choices: How the manager feels about the report
A guess about how the period will end
What happened against each expectation
items.explanation: It restates facts against the written plan.

items.prompt: In Outcome A, how is the PIP closed?
choices: In writing, citing the met expectations
Verbally, with nothing at all put into a record
By opening a second PIP right away
items.explanation: A written close ends the plan clearly.

items.prompt: In Outcome B, what does the note do?
choices: Softens the facts so that nobody's feelings get hurt
Says which expectation was missed, and by how much
Holds the misses back until the very end
items.explanation: Plain facts are fairest for everyone.

items.prompt: What does expectation 1 allow for lateness?
choices: Up to two days, at the manager's discretion
Anything under a week's slip, if flagged
None; any lateness fails it
items.explanation: It is a yes/no rule: on or before the date.

items.prompt: What should happen after a successful PIP?
choices: Stop taking notes immediately
Keep recording going forward
Delete the old record
items.explanation: A recurring pattern should not restart from zero.

items.prompt: What should the manager involve in Outcome B?
choices: HR and the company's process
A different team's manager
A team-wide announcement of it
items.explanation: The next step follows company policy.

items.prompt: What belongs in the PIP besides expectations?
choices: A comparison with teammates
A ranking of the report's skills
Checkpoints and the support offered
items.explanation: The plan includes dates and the help provided.

items.prompt: What does a mid-point checkpoint give the report?
choices: A surprise held back until the end
A clear view of where they stand
A final decision
items.explanation: It makes progress visible before the final review.

items.prompt: At the Jun 15 checkpoint the release has not shipped and no risk was flagged. Which note is best?
choices: The report is still not treating this plan with the seriousness that it deserves
The release is late again, which shows a continuing lack of commitment overall
The report did not meet the plan and the pattern of behavior is unchanged
Release not ready on its date, no flag filed: expectations 1 and 3 not met
items.explanation: The best note states observable facts tied to numbered expectations. The others state attitude or conclusion.
items.reference:
Checkpoint note
fact: release shipped 3 days after the date
fact: no risk flag filed
tie to: expectations 1 and 3
avoid: 'not taking this seriously'
Why: a note of facts against numbered expectations is checkable and fair to both sides.
items.learnMore:
Writing the checkpoint note

State what happened, tie it to the numbered expectation, and keep the tone the same in either outcome. When the expectations are checkable, so is the note.

Common mistake

Replacing facts with conclusions about attitude, which reopens the subjective argument.
items.reflection: Imagine you were the report. What would you want a checkpoint note about your progress to say, and what would make it feel fair even if the news was bad?

items.prompt: The report says the June 15 release slipped because a vendor delayed an input, and they flagged it 4 business days early. What should the manager do?
choices: Ignore the flag, since expectation 1 fails on lateness whatever the cause
Check the written flag, judge expectation 3 on it, review the cause for 1
Treat the flag as proof the report is simply making excuses again
Extend the whole plan without first looking at what was filed
items.explanation: Expectation 3 asks for a written early flag, so the record decides it. Expectation 1 may need a fair look at the cause.

items.prompt: A report in their first weeks at the company is placed on a standard 30-day PIP. Which concern applies most strongly?
choices: The plan is too short to measure anything fairly, whatever the person's role
Probation or notice rules may override the usual sequence, so check with HR first
The sequence applies identically whatever the person's length of service
Documentation is unnecessary for someone who is so new to the role itself
items.explanation: Tenure and local rules change what process is required. This is a case where the standard sequence may not be the right tool.
